# Cūḷasuññata Sutta (MN 121 (PTS MN iii 104))

**ID:** MN 121 (PTS MN iii 104)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Cūḷasuññata Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Shorter Discourse on Emptiness
**PTS:** MN iii 104
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷasuññata Sutta* ("The Shorter Discourse on Emptiness", MN 121) is a foundational discourse on Buddhist meditation in which the Buddha explains to the Venerable Ānanda what it means to dwell in genuine, undistorted emptiness (*suññatā*) [Anālayo 2010; Rogell 2003]. Initiated by Ānanda's recollection that the Buddha often dwells in emptiness, the discourse outlines a gradual meditative progression [Anālayo 2010, 2017; Brunnholz 2015]. The instruction guides the practitioner from noticing that a physical location is empty of what is absent yet not empty of what remains present, moving through progressive mental purifications based on the perceptions of wilderness, earth, the immaterial spheres, and signless concentration of mind (*animitta cetosamādhi*) [Anālayo 2010, 2017; Polak 2011]. This step-by-step meditative descent culminates in the destruction of the taints (*āsava*)—the fruitional attainment of arahantship—at which point the text specifically applies the abstract noun *suññatā* [Anālayo 2010; Brunnholz 2015].

The formulation in the sutta—that one sees what is absent as empty and accurately cognizes what remains as truly present—played an important role in later Buddhist philosophy [Nagao 1991]. This canonical definition of emptiness was widely cited and adapted as an authoritative prooftext by the Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda and Tathāgatagarbha traditions, directly influencing texts such as the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* [Deleanu 2006; Nagao 1991].

Canonical parallels to the discourse survive in Chinese translation in the *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 190, *Xiao kong jing*, T 26) and in the Tibetan Kangyur as the *Śūnyatānāmamahāsūtra* (D 290, *mDo chen po ston pa nyid*) [Brunnholz 2015; Deleanu 2006; PIATS-06-Fagernes-1992]. DharmaNexus aligns MN 121 directly with fascicle 49 of the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (T 26) and reveals extensive Pali-internal text reuse with other discourses on meditative attainments, sharing large textual passages with the *Navakanipāta* of the Aṅguttaranikāya (AN 9), the *Mahāsuññata Sutta* (MN 122), and the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* [DharmaNexus].
